agree.reason: The open budget and the frank admission of being a first-time creator would win some trust, but a backer who has already lost $85 gets no delivery date, no refund promise and no update schedule, so they may well hold back.

honest.reason: It rightly avoids calling the game a 'proven hit', but it says the leftover $5,400 'covers' platform fees when 10% fees come to about $2,800, and it presents the 23 ratings as coming from real players without saying most were people who played at the designer's own convention table.

works_the_facts.reason: Working out 572 backers and setting that against the 1,240 sign-ups is good, but the budget is muddled: the $5,400 remainder only appears if you work out 572 × $9 shipping yourself, and about $2,600 of it is never accounted for.

right_comparison.reason: It gives an honest picture of what happens if funding falls short (the game stays on the designer's table), but it never sets the backer's choice against the risk of the game never shipping, which is the comparison this reader actually makes.

qualification.reason: There is no November delivery date, no promise of a refund if delivery is three months late, and no commitment to updates every two weeks, so the backer has nothing dated or checkable to hold the creator to.

objections.reason: It deals with the 'first-time creator' doubt through the playtesting and the factory quote, but it leaves out the facts that answer the 'will it ever ship' fear: the signed quote, the finished art and rules, the refund pledge, the update schedule and the reviewer's launch-week video.

fit.reason: It is a crowdfunding pitch of about 500 words with a hook, clear sections and a closing appeal, which is the form the brief asked for.
